title: Solar PV in a conservation area or on a listed building
subtitle: Understanding when permitted development rights apply and when you need full planning permission
excerpt: Solar panels on most UK houses are permitted development and need no planning application. Conservation areas and listed buildings are different: panels on a principal elevation visible from a highway always need permission in a conservation area, and any works to a listed building need listed building consent. Knowing the rules before you buy the system avoids enforcement action.
sourceNotes: Town and Country Planning (General Permitted Development) (England) Order 2015 Schedule 2 Part 14; Historic England advice on solar panels and listed buildings (2023); Planning Practice Guidance on renewable energy.

glossaryTerms.definition: Planning permission granted automatically by national legislation for certain types of work, without requiring a formal application to the local planning authority.
Solar photovoltaic panels that convert sunlight into electricity directly, as distinct from solar thermal collectors that heat water.

A separate consent required for any works to a listed building (Grade I, II* or II) that affects its character as a building of special architectural or historic interest. Distinct from planning permission.

content.text: Solar panels on a standard house in England are
permitted development

under Schedule 2 Part 14 of the GPDO 2015. No planning application is needed as long as the panels meet the conditions: not on a wall or roof slope that fronts a highway, protrude no more than 200 mm from the roof surface, and are removed when no longer required.

Conservation areas and listed buildings lose some or all of these permitted development rights. Getting the rules wrong before installation means you may be required to remove a completed system at your own cost.
Conservation areas
In a conservation area,
solar PV

panels are still permitted development. But this only applies to roof slopes and walls that do not face a highway and are not visible from one. A rear-facing roof is excluded from permitted development if the lane behind the garden is a public highway.
North-facing rear roof not visible from any road: permitted development usually applies here.
A south-facing front roof visible from the street: requires full planning permission in a conservation area.
Flat roofs: if the panels would be visible from a highway, planning permission is required.
Listed buildings
Any works to a listed building that affect its character require
listed building consent

, in addition to any planning permission needed. This applies even if the works would otherwise be permitted development. Attaching solar panels to a listed building almost always requires listed building consent. The fixing of brackets to the historic fabric affects the building's character.

The best approach is a pre-application consultation with the local planning authority (LPA). Many LPAs will indicate at pre-app whether a scheme is likely to be acceptable. This is worth the fee before commissioning an installation.
When applications are likely to succeed

Rear roof slopes not visible from the street. Many LPAs will grant consent for panels on a non-prominent slope, even in a conservation area or on a listed building. The brackets must avoid drilling into historic mortar joints, and panels should be set back from the ridge.

Building-integrated photovoltaics (BIPV): solar slates and tiles that replace the existing roof covering are often more acceptable than bolt-on panels. They cost more but reduce the visual impact, which is the main LPA concern.

Ground-mounted systems in a rear garden away from the street. A ground-mounted system at the back of a listed building's plot is assessed on landscape impact rather than impact on the listed structure; consent is often easier to obtain.
Scotland, Wales, Northern Ireland

Scotland, Wales, and Northern Ireland have their own planning rules. The basic approach to solar panels is similar to England, but the thresholds and conservation area rules differ. In Wales, check the relevant Technical Advice Notes. In Scotland, check Planning Advice Notes. In Northern Ireland, check Planning Policy Statements. Always confirm the local rules before proceeding.

rows.symptom: Local authority enforcement notice received after installation
rows.cause: Panels installed as permitted development on a slope that requires consent in the conservation area
rows.fix: Seek retrospective planning permission immediately, a retrospective application has a reasonable chance of success if the panels are on a rear slope with limited visual impact. Remove only if required by a formal enforcement notice.

rows.symptom: Listed building consent refused for solar panels on main roof
rows.cause: LPA judged that panels on the principal elevation are harmful to the listed building's character
rows.fix: Reapply for a rear-elevation scheme or a ground-mounted system; consider BIPV solar slates if the roof needs re-covering anyway.
